    How an ATS Checker Reads Your Resume (and Why Good Resumes Still Get Missed)

    By ATS Score Checker Free Editorial TeamUpdated October 31, 2026 8 min read

    You can be an excellent candidate with a well-written resume and still be invisible in an applicant tracking system. The reason is usually not your experience — it is how the software reads the file. An ATS checker simulates that reading step so you can catch problems before a real system does. Here is what happens when you click "Upload".

    Step 1: Text extraction

    The ATS first pulls raw text out of your file. With a DOCX, it reads the document's underlying XML. With a PDF, it reads the text layer — the characters and their positions on the page. If there is no text layer (a scanned page or a resume exported as an image), there is nothing to read and many systems will store an almost empty profile.

    Quick test

    Open your PDF and try to select a sentence with your cursor. If you cannot highlight individual words, the ATS cannot read them either.

    Step 2: Reading order

    Next the parser decides what order the text belongs in. People read a two-column resume left column first, then right. Software often reads straight across the page, line by line, interleaving the two columns. Your sidebar skills end up glued to the middle of a job description, and dates float away from the roles they belong to.

    Tables cause similar trouble: some parsers read cell by cell, others row by row, and some skip table content entirely. Text boxes and shapes are frequently ignored.

    Step 3: Section detection

    Once the text is in order, the system looks for headings to split it into sections. It recognises common labels — Summary, Experience, Work History, Education, Skills, Certifications, Projects. A heading like "My Journey" or an icon instead of a word gives it nothing to match, so your entire work history may be filed under the wrong section or dropped into a generic notes field.

    Step 4: Field extraction

    Within each section the parser tries to identify entities: job title, employer, location, start date, end date, degree, institution, skill names. Consistency helps enormously here.

    • Use one date format throughout, such as "Jan 2023 – Mar 2025" or "01/2023 – 03/2025".
    • Put the job title and employer on predictable lines, in the same order for every role.
    • Write "Present" for current roles rather than leaving the end date blank.
    • Spell out abbreviations at least once: "Search Engine Optimization (SEO)".

    Step 5: Search and ranking

    Finally, your structured profile sits in a database alongside every other applicant. Recruiters filter and search it, and some systems score candidates against the job requirements. This is where keywords matter: if the role requires "Python" and "data pipelines" and neither appears in your extracted text, you will not show up in that search — even if you have done exactly that work.

    Formatting choices that commonly break parsing

    ElementRiskSafer alternative
    Two or three columnsText read out of orderSingle column, left-aligned
    Tables for layoutCells skipped or mergedPlain lines with consistent spacing
    Contact info in header/footerName and email not capturedContact block at top of body
    Icons for phone/emailIcons become garbage charactersWrite "Email:" and "Phone:"
    Skill bars or rating chartsImages carry no textList skills as words
    Unusual fontsCharacters mis-mappedArial, Calibri, Georgia, Helvetica
    Creative headingsSection not detectedExperience, Education, Skills

    The 5-minute self-test

    1. Select all the text in your resume and paste it into Notepad or any plain text editor.
    2. Check that your name, email and phone appear at the top.
    3. Read through: is each job title next to its employer and dates?
    4. Confirm every section heading is present as a word.
    5. Run the same file through our ATS checker and compare its section and formatting findings with what you saw.

    If the plain-text version reads cleanly, you have solved the hardest part. From there, improvements come from content and keywords — covered in our guides to writing stronger bullet points and tailoring with a resume score checker.

    Does a beautiful design hurt you?

    Not always. Many modern systems handle reasonable designs well, and a visually polished resume helps once a human is reading it. The safe approach is to keep two versions: a clean, single-column version for online applications and ATS portals, and a designed version for networking, email introductions and interviews.

    Frequently asked questions

    Can an ATS read a PDF resume?

    Yes, most modern systems read text-based PDFs well. Problems arise with scanned PDFs (images of text), PDFs exported from design tools with text converted to outlines, and complex multi-column layouts.

    Is DOCX or PDF better for an ATS?

    Both work when they are simple and text-based. Follow the employer's instructions if they specify a format; otherwise a clean PDF preserves your layout and a DOCX is the safest fallback for older systems.

    Do ATS systems read headers and footers?

    Some do, many do not reliably. Keep your name and contact details in the main body of the document.
